title: The judge who found English's lost cousins
text: In 1786 William Jones, a British judge in Calcutta, told the Asiatic Society that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin were too alike to be a coincidence. They must have sprung from a common source that no longer existed, and Gothic, Celtic and Persian probably did too. That lost source is now called Proto-Indo-European.
source: William Jones, Third Anniversary Discourse to the Asiatic Society (1786); Wikipedia, William Jones (philologist)
more:
Jones wasn't the first to notice the resemblances, and he got some things wrong, lumping in languages like Egyptian and Japanese. But his lecture caught the moment and launched comparative linguistics.

The family he pointed to now includes most languages of Europe, Iran and northern India, from Hindi to Welsh to English. Nearly half the world's people speak one natively.

No one ever wrote Proto-Indo-European down. It was spoken roughly five or six thousand years ago, and everything we know about it has been reconstructed by comparing its descendants. This thread follows one branch of that family all the way to the English you're reading now.

title: Why father sounds like pater
text: Latin pater, English father. Latin pes, ped-, English foot. Latin tres, English three. The pattern is regular: where Latin and Greek kept an old p or t, the Germanic languages shifted it to f or th. Rasmus Rask spotted it, and Jacob Grimm, of the fairy tales, laid it out in 1822.
source: Jacob Grimm, Deutsche Grammatik (1822); Wikipedia, Grimm's law
more:
Grimm's law describes a set of consonant changes that happened in the ancestor of the Germanic languages, probably in the first millennium BC. P became f, t became th, k became h, and other stops shifted in step.

It explains pairs that look unrelated at first: Latin cornu and English horn, Latin piscis and English fish. It's also why English often has two versions of one root, a native word and a later borrowing from Latin: father and paternal, foot and pedal.

The big lesson was that sound change isn't random. It follows rules, which turned the study of language into something closer to a science.

title: English arrived by boat
text: English was not born in England. It came over with Germanic settlers, the Angles, Saxons and their neighbours, who crossed the North Sea in the mid-5th century. Their language, Old English, is so different from ours that the opening of Beowulf, which begins Hwaet!, needs a translation.
source: Wikipedia, Old English; Beowulf
more:
The name itself is a souvenir of the migration: English comes from the Angles, and England was once Englaland, land of the Angles.

The only manuscript of Beowulf was copied around 975 to 1025 and nearly burned in a library fire in 1731. Its language had grammatical endings much like modern German, and letters we have since lost, such as thorn and ash.

The Celtic languages already spoken in Britain left surprisingly few words in English, mostly place and river names, like Thames and Avon. What would really reshape English was the next wave of invaders, who spoke a close cousin of Old English.

title: The Vikings gave us they
text: Viking settlers in England left behind some of the most basic words we have: they, them and their, plus egg, knife, skin and sky, which in Old Norse meant cloud. Window comes from vindauga, literally wind-eye.
source: Wikipedia, List of English words of Old Norse origin (citing the Online Etymology Dictionary)
more:
Norse speakers settled across northern and eastern England from the 9th to the 11th centuries, in the region called the Danelaw. Old English and Old Norse were close enough that neighbours could probably get the gist of each other.

Borrowing nouns is common when cultures meet. Borrowing pronouns is rare, and it shows how deeply the two populations blended in daily life.

Some scholars think this mixing also helped English shed many of its grammatical endings. When two related languages share roots but differ in endings, speakers tend to drop the endings and lean on word order instead. Then, in 1066, a very different set of invaders arrived.

text: And swine is good Saxon... and pork, I think, is good Norman-French; and so when the brute lives, and is in the charge of a Saxon slave, she goes by her Saxon name; but becomes a Norman, and is called pork, when she is carried to the Castle-hall to feast among the nobles...
author: Walter Scott
source: Ivanhoe, ch. 1 (1819)
more:
Wamba the jester is explaining to Gurth the swineherd how the Norman Conquest of 1066 split their language. The animals tended by English peasants kept their Old English names: swine, cow, sheep, calf. The meat served to the French-speaking lords took French names: pork, beef, mutton, veal.

Scott was a novelist, not a linguist, and the real story is messier, but the pattern is real and it runs through English. Plain, everyday words tend to be Germanic. Fancier words of law, government and food often came through French: begin versus commence, ask versus inquire.

For about three centuries, the people running England spoke French.

title: Why English spelling looks so wrong
text: Between about 1400 and 1700, the long vowels of English moved. Bite was once said roughly like beet, and house roughly like hoose. Spelling had started settling down around the same time, partly thanks to printers, so we're still writing many words the way they sounded before the Great Vowel Shift.
source: Wikipedia, Great Vowel Shift
more:
This is the main reason English vowel letters behave so strangely compared with Spanish, Italian or German, where a written i still sounds like ee. Chaucer, writing in the late 1300s, would have pronounced name with a vowel like the a in father.

Nobody fully knows why the shift happened. Theories include the social mixing after the Black Death and the rise of London as a centre that blended regional accents.

The press gets some of the blame for the mismatch too. Early printers, some of them Flemish, fixed spellings while pronunciation was still on the move, and some of those spellings stuck long after the sounds had changed.

text: ...sounds are too volatile and subtile for legal restraints; to enchain syllables, and to lash the wind, are equally the undertakings of pride, unwilling to measure its desires by its strength.
author: Samuel Johnson
source: Preface to A Dictionary of the English Language (1755)
more:
Johnson worked on his Dictionary from 1746 to 1755, with only a few clerks to help copy out quotations. He began half hoping to fix English in place, the way the French Academy tried to guard French. By the end he'd given up on that. Language, he decided, can be recorded but not frozen.

That's the lesson of this whole thread. English started as a dialect of Germanic settlers, borrowed pronouns from Vikings and vocabulary from Normans, and rearranged its vowels while printers weren't looking. It never stopped moving.

Every new slang word you dislike is part of the same story.

title: Nice used to be an insult
text: Nice comes, through Old French, from Latin nescius, meaning ignorant or not knowing. When it entered English in the Middle Ages, calling someone nice meant they were foolish or simple. Over the centuries it drifted through shy, fussy and precise before landing on pleasant.
source: Wiktionary, nice (etymology); Online Etymology Dictionary, nice
more:
Words often slide in meaning, but nice made an unusually long trip. The Latin root is ne, not, plus scire, to know, the same scire that gives us science. So nice and science are distant opposites.

In Shakespeare's time nice often meant precise or finely balanced, a sense that survives in phrases like a nice distinction. The pleasant, agreeable meaning only took over in the 1700s.

Linguists call this kind of upgrade amelioration. The reverse, pejoration, happened to silly, which once meant blessed or happy, and to awful, which once meant full of awe.

title: Your muscles are little mice
text: Muscle comes from the Latin musculus, which literally means little mouse. Romans thought a flexing muscle, especially a bicep rippling under the skin, looked like a small mouse moving around. The same Latin word also meant mussel, the shellfish.
source: Wiktionary, muscle (etymology), from Latin musculus, diminutive of mus, mouse
more:
The image was common in the ancient world. Greek used mys for both mouse and muscle, and several other languages make the same link.

Mus, mouse, is a very old Indo-European root. It's related to English mouse itself, through the sound changes covered in the How English became English thread.

Mussel took a separate road into English but comes from the same diminutive, probably because the dark shellfish looked mouse-like too. So when someone at the gym shows off their muscles, they are, etymologically speaking, showing you their mice.

text: Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested...
author: Francis Bacon
source: Essays, Of Studies (1625 edition)
more:
Bacon goes on to explain the metaphor: some books you dip into, some you read through without great care, and a few you read wholly, with diligence and attention. He even allows that some can be read by deputy, through someone else's summary.

That's surprisingly modern advice. Bacon isn't telling you to finish every book you start. He's telling you to match your attention to the book's worth.

The same short essay contains another famous line: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man. Reading fills you up, conversation makes you quick, and writing forces you to be precise.

text: Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts.
author: William Strunk Jr.
source: The Elements of Style, rule 13, Omit needless words (1918)
more:
William Strunk was an English professor at Cornell who privately printed this little guide for his students. One of them, E. B. White, later revised and expanded it, and the Strunk and White version became one of the bestselling writing guides ever.

The passage continues with an important clarification: this doesn't mean every sentence must be short or that detail must go. It means every word should tell.

That's the part people forget. Concise isn't the same as terse. A long sentence can be concise if each word earns its place, and a short one can be padded. The test is whether anything could be cut without losing meaning.

text: Books are the treasured wealth of the world and the fit inheritance of generations and nations.
author: Henry David Thoreau
source: Walden, ch. 3, Reading (1854)
more:
Thoreau wrote this in his cabin at Walden Pond, where he lived from 1845 to 1847, trying to strip life to its essentials. Among the few things he decided were worth keeping were the classics.

The chapter is a demanding one. He argues that most people read only easy books and never learn to read in the higher sense, the kind of reading you have to stand on tiptoe for. He wanted people to tackle Homer and Aeschylus, ideally in the original.

You don't have to agree with his snobbery to like the core idea: the best books are a shared inheritance, and nobody needs permission to claim it.

text: The person, be it gentleman or lady, who has not pleasure in a good novel, must be intolerably stupid.
author: Jane Austen
source: Northanger Abbey, ch. 14 (1817)
more:
Henry Tilney says this to Catherine Morland, who assumed a clever young man would look down on novels. In Austen's day many people did. Novels were seen as frivolous, the junk food of reading, especially for young women.

Austen had none of it. Earlier in the same book she steps out of the story to defend novels directly as works in which the greatest powers of the mind are displayed.

Northanger Abbey is itself a joke about reading: Catherine has devoured so many Gothic thrillers that she starts imagining murders in a perfectly ordinary country house. It was written in the late 1790s but only published after Austen's death.

text: No man but a blockhead ever wrote, except for money.
author: Samuel Johnson
source: James Boswell, The Life of Samuel Johnson, entry for 1776 (1791)
more:
Johnson really did say it, according to his friend and biographer James Boswell, who was writing down his conversation as it happened. Boswell immediately pushes back, calling it a strange opinion that Johnson's lazy streak made him utter, and noting that the history of literature is full of counterexamples.

Johnson knew the subject. He grew up poor, came to London nearly penniless, and wrote for hire for years: essays, reviews, parliamentary reports, a dictionary.

The line still provokes because it's half right. Plenty of great work has been written for love. But a lot of it, including Johnson's own, got finished because someone was waiting to pay for it.

text: The etymologist finds the deadest word to have been once a brilliant picture. Language is fossil poetry.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
source: Essays: Second Series, The Poet (1844)
more:
Emerson's idea is that every word began as someone's fresh image. Over time, with heavy use, the image wears away and only the plain meaning is left, the way limestone is made of countless tiny shells that no longer look like shells.

Etymology lets you crack the stone open. Muscle was a little mouse. Window was a wind-eye. Disaster means a bad star, from a time when misfortune was blamed on the planets. Daisy is the day's eye, because it opens in the morning.

Once you start noticing, ordinary speech is full of these buried pictures, and it becomes hard to call any word dull.

title: The curse of knowledge
text: Steven Pinker argues the main reason writing is hard to read isn't that authors want to show off. It's that they can't imagine not knowing what they know. They skip steps, use jargon and drop terms without explaining them, because once you understand something, it's very hard to remember what it was like not to.
author: Steven Pinker
source: The Sense of Style, ch. 3 (2014)
more:
Psychologists call this the curse of knowledge, and it shows up in experiments everywhere. People who tap out a tune expect listeners to name it far more often than they actually can, because the tapper hears the melody in their head.

Pinker's fix is not simply to imagine your reader, since the curse makes that hard. It's to show drafts to real people, and to reread your own work after enough time has passed that you've partly forgotten it.

He also suggests a better mental picture: write as though you're helping a smart friend see something, rather than proving you're clever. It applies to emails as much as books.

title: Bad writing hides bad thinking
text: George Orwell argued that sloppy language and sloppy thought feed each other. Stale phrases and vague abstractions let writers avoid deciding what they mean, and let politicians describe ugly things without calling up mental pictures. His fix: prefer short, plain, concrete words, cut what you can, and use the active voice.
author: George Orwell
source: Politics and the English Language (1946)
more:
Orwell's examples were political. Bombing villages and driving out their inhabitants could be described in a bloodless phrase that sounded technical and spared the reader any image of what actually happened. Euphemism, he thought, was a way of defending the indefensible.

He offered six rules, all versions of the same instinct: don't reach for a ready-made phrase or a long word when a short, plain one will do. The last rule was an escape hatch: drop any of the others rather than write something ugly.

The essay is worth reading in full. It's short, and it practises what it preaches.

title: Read a lot, write a lot
text: Stephen King says there's no shortcut to writing well: you have to read a lot and write a lot. Reading shows you what works and, just as useful, what doesn't. He's also suspicious of adverbs, which he sees as a sign the writer doesn't trust the sentence to carry its meaning.
author: Stephen King
source: On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft (2000)
more:
On Writing is half memoir, half manual, and it was finished after King was hit by a van in 1999 and nearly killed. That gives the advice an unusual urgency.

He reads constantly, in waiting rooms, at meals, on the treadmill, and argues that a writer who claims to be too busy to read has given up the main tool of the trade. Bad books, he says, teach you as much as good ones, because they show you exactly what to avoid.

His adverb rule is about confidence. If he answered angrily is needed, the dialogue itself probably isn't doing its job. Fix the sentence instead of propping it up.

title: Who put the b in debt?
text: Nobody pronounces the b in debt, and for centuries nobody wrote it either. So where did it come from?
source: Wiktionary, debt (etymology)
more:
It was added on purpose, by scholars. English borrowed the word from Old French dette, and in Middle English it was spelled dette or det, matching how it sounded.

During the Renaissance, writers who admired Latin started tweaking English spellings to show off a word's classical roots. Since dette came ultimately from Latin debitum, what is owed, they slipped in a b. Nobody ever started saying it.

The same fashion gave doubt its b, from Latin dubitare, and receipt its p, from recipere. Some of these respellings were even wrong: island got its s by mistaken analogy with isle, though the word is native English, from Old English igland.

title: Where did OK come from?
text: OK may be the most widely understood word on the planet. It first appeared in print in a Boston newspaper in 1839. What did the two letters originally stand for?
source: Wikipedia, OK (citing Allen Walker Read's studies)
more:
Oll korrect, a deliberately misspelled all correct. In the late 1830s, Boston newspapers had a fad for jokey abbreviations of deliberately misspelled phrases. Almost all of them died. OK survived.

The linguist Allen Walker Read traced this origin in a series of articles in the 1960s, finding the first printed use in the Boston Morning Post on 23 March 1839.

What saved it was the 1840 presidential election. Democrats claimed it stood for Old Kinderhook, a nickname for President Martin Van Buren, who came from Kinderhook, New York. Vote for OK was a catchy slogan, and the term went national. From there it went everywhere, eventually into dozens of other languages.
